lead: We Made a Drone Fly — Now It's Your Turn
sub: A one-button app already flies the Mini 4 Pro from our own code. That's your launch pad — build your own idea on top of it.

title: Flying Safely — Before You Arm the Motors
desc: Under 250 g is not harmless — and your own code bypasses the guardrails DJI Fly enforces

items: Indoors: propeller guards mandatory, no exceptions — props at ~14,000 rpm cut skin and eyes
Indoors: no GPS — the drone drifts on optical flow alone; keep ≥ 2 m clearance to walls, windows, lamps
Outdoors: 120 m above ground is the ceiling for the whole Open category — a narrow allowance exists near obstacles over 105 m tall, don't plan around it
Outdoors: check DiPUL first — airports, hospitals, prisons and nature reserves are geo-zones (maptool-dipul.dfs.de, Module 14)
Nobody under or behind the drone during takeoff, landing or a virtual-stick test — that's exactly where a code bug puts it
Say "props spinning" out loud before arming; hand stays on the RC even during an autonomous mission
Anyone not briefed and not consenting is an uninvolved person — never overflown (A1, Module 1)
Virtual stick is the dangerous mode — the aircraft obeys your loop, not the pilot; build in a timeout / deadman check
DJI Fly's limits are not the law — the app ceiling is configurable and your own SDK code bypasses it entirely
Props off + enableSimulator first, then indoors with guards — your code never flies outdoors (Module 2)
Know the abort path before takeoff: RC pause > left stick down > power cut — misbehaves? Land immediately
Everything on this slide has one price tag: as pilot you are the personally liable operator (Module 2)

title: One Button. A Full Mission.
desc: labs/dji-hello-world — a real app that flies a real drone

items: A single screen with one green button: FLY MISSION
Press it → the Mini 4 Pro takes off, flies ~1.5 m forward, spins 180°, flies ~1.5 m back, and lands — entirely on its own
~400 lines of Kotlin on the DJI Mobile SDK v5, built in a couple of hours
Code & full write-up: labs/dji-hello-world
This is the proof of concept your whole project builds on — the old question "can we even control a DJI drone from code?" is already answered: yes
You inherit registration, connection, KeyManager reads, virtual-stick control and landing — the hard part is done

title: DJI SDK Architecture: Four Managers, One Aircraft
desc: Your code never touches the drone — it asks a manager on the phone, and the answer comes back later

body.alt: Your app on the phone calls four DJI SDK managers, which reach the aircraft through the remote controller: USB cable, then radio link. The flight controller decides who flies, and the pilot can take over at the remote controller
body.caption: Drawn from the class signatures in MSDK 5.18.0, the version the lab app builds against — the next two slides show the same SDK as UML

items: Your code runs on the phone, not on the drone — every command crosses a USB cable and a radio link; if either drops, your loop keeps running and nothing arrives

Control is on loan — the flight controller hands it to your code and takes it back: link lost, pause button, mode switch, low battery, near a geo-zone boundary. The drone then follows its own settings, not your loop (Module 2)
There is no drone object — each capability is a singleton manager you reach with getInstance(); the lab app uses these four out of about 35 in the SDK
The simulator lives in the flight controller — so it needs the real drone switched on, props off (Module 2)

title: The Managers in UML: Interface, Singleton, Callback
desc: The managers the lab app uses share one shape — learn it once and most of the SDK reads the same way

body.alt: UML class diagram: SDKManager, VirtualStickManager and SimulatorManager each implement an interface, and answer through callback interfaces that fail with an IDJIError
body.caption: Dashed line with triangle: implements · dashed arrow: uses · only the methods the lab app needs are listed · CompletionCallback is nested in CommonCallbacks

items: Interface + singleton: each manager is one class implementing an interface of the same name, and getInstance() is the only way in — most of the SDK's managers follow this pattern

Commands are asynchronous: enableVirtualStick(callback) returns at once; later the SDK calls onSuccess() or onFailure(error). Wait for onSuccess before the next step — if you skip that, your loop steers a drone that never accepted the command

Movement commands give no feedback: setting rightStick.verticalPosition or calling sendVirtualStickAdvancedParam(param) has no callback and no return value — to know the drone really moved, read its position back through KeyManager

title: The Key Model in UML: One Manager for Every Value
desc: Telemetry and commands are not methods — they are constants, and KeyManager is the only door to them

body.alt: UML class diagram: key classes hold DJIKeyInfo constants, KeyTools turns one into a DJIKey, and KeyManager reads, writes, listens to or fires it
body.caption: Solid line with triangle: extends · dashed arrow: uses · three of several hundred constants shown; BatteryKey, ProductKey, CameraKey have the same shape

body.card: Follow one call through the diagram
items: Pick a constant on a key class — FlightControllerKey.KeyIsFlying is a DJIKeyInfo; wrap it with KeyTools.createKey to get a DJIKey; hand it to KeyManager
Commands are the action variants: KeyStartTakeoff is a DJIActionKeyInfo, becomes an ActionKey, and goes to performAction — the code is on the next slide

title: Keys, Not Methods — and Every Answer Comes Later
desc: The two SDK conventions to know before you read or generate a single line of flight code

body.code: // a value: pick a key constant, make it addressable, hand it to KeyManager val sats = KeyTools.createKey(FlightControllerKey.KeyGPSSatelliteCount) KeyManager.getInstance().listen(sats, this) { old, new -> logLine("satellites: $old → $new") } // a command is a key too — and this call returns before the drone has done anything KeyManager.getInstance().performAction( KeyTools.createKey(FlightControllerKey.KeyStartTakeoff), object : CommonCallbacks.CompletionCallbackWithParam<EmptyMsg> { override fun onSuccess(t: EmptyMsg?) { /* takeoff accepted — now wait until it is flying */ } override fun onFailure(e: IDJIError) { /* the mission ends here */ } })

items: No getAltitude(), no takeOff() — every value and command is a constant on a key class (FlightControllerKey, BatteryKey, ProductKey…); KeyManager reads, writes, listens to or fires it
A command does not return its result — the outcome arrives in onSuccess / onFailure; the lab app waits for it with a timeout before the next step
If generated code calls drone.takeOff(), it was invented — check every SDK call against the API reference
Two ways to steer, same manager: stick positions (the lab app) or sendVirtualStickAdvancedParam with velocities (Module 2's bug slide)

title: The Code You Inherit: One Hop, One Turn
desc: MainActivity.kt, condensed — open-loop hops, closed-loop yaw, and the deadman that makes both survivable

body.code: private const val FORWARD_STICK = 70 // ~10 % stick — gentle private const val FORWARD_MS = 1000L // ~1 s powered, coasts to ~1.5 m private const val YAW_TIMEOUT_MS = 15000L step("Flying ~1.5 m forward…") VirtualStickManager.getInstance().rightStick.verticalPosition = FORWARD_STICK sleepChecked(FORWARD_MS) // throws if STOP was pressed zeroSticks() // the hop ends here, whatever happened private fun rotate180() { val target = normalizeDeg(heading() + 180.0) VirtualStickManager.getInstance().leftStick.horizontalPosition = YAW_STICK val deadline = System.currentTimeMillis() + YAW_TIMEOUT_MS try { while (System.currentTimeMillis() < deadline) { checkAbort() if (abs(normalizeDeg(heading() - target)) < YAW_TOLERANCE_DEG) break Thread.sleep(50) } } finally { zeroSticks() } // the deadman: sticks go to 0 on ANY exit }

body.card: Read it like a safety reviewer
items: Bounded: the hop is a fixed FORWARD_MS, the turn has a deadline — nothing runs until 'done', everything runs until 'done or time is up'
Abortable: sleepChecked and checkAbort throw when STOP is pressed; the handler zeroes the sticks and starts auto-landing
Zero on exit: the finally is the whole safety story — an exception mid-turn must not leave a yaw command live (Module 2's second bug)
Open loop: 1.5 m is a guess from stick and time, not a measurement. Project idea #13 closes that loop with telemetry — the fix for Module 2's 'fly forward 2 m'

title: Everything That Fought Back
desc: First flight took a dozen rebuilds — every single layer resisted

rows: Build died with a connection timeout
The school network blocked the SDK downloads — a mobile hotspot fixed it
DJI Fly refused to connect to the drone
Outdated firmware — update the aircraft in DJI Fly first
App vanished the instant it launched
NoClassDefFoundError — the SDK secretly needs AndroidX on the classpath
Plugged in the phone — nothing happened
We used the RC's charging port; the data port is next to the clamp
"Waiting for drone" forever
The RC wasn't linked to the drone — you pair it once via DJI Fly
request_handler_not_found on takeoff
The drone had gone to sleep — power-cycle, wait for FC connected: true
compass_large_mode outside
Magnetic interference — step away from metal, then it flew

items: Every one of these is written down so you skip the pain — the complete troubleshooting log lives in labs/dji-hello-world

title: What the DJI SDK Actually Gives You
desc: The Mobile SDK v5 exposes the aircraft as a set of programmable interfaces — here is the surface you build on

items: Takeoff, landing, return-to-home as direct commands
Virtual Stick — synthesise stick input to fly the aircraft from code; on this drone it is the only way to fly a route
Adjust settings — shutter, ISO, aperture, exposure
Capture photos and video; point the gimbal from code
Pull the live video feed into your app for image processing
Subscribe via KeyManager to GPS, altitude, attitude, velocity
Battery, satellites, link status in real time (up to ~10 Hz)
Read obstacle-avoidance state — distances and warnings from the vision system
Browse and download photos / video from the aircraft's storage
The old ActiveTrack / TapFly / Point-of-Interest modes are not exposed as SDK-controllable missions on consumer drones like the Mini 4 Pro
No waypoint missions either: routes that the aircraft stores and flies on its own are in the SDK for enterprise models only — here your phone steers every metre, so a dropped link ends the route
You get the building blocks (virtual stick, telemetry, video) — you build the intelligence yourself

body.card: First 30 minutes in the lab — props off, drone on the desk
items: Build and install the app on the phone; connect via the RC's data port and wait for FC connected: true in the log
Enable the simulator (SimulatorManager.enableSimulator, README §4) — the flight controller now flies a virtual aircraft
Read one value from KeyManager — KeyGPSSatelliteCount or KeyAircraftLocation3D — and log it every second: your first telemetry
Press FLY MISSION and watch the step() lines scroll: takeoff, hop, turn, hop, landing — in the simulator, nothing moves but the numbers
Hand in: a screenshot of that log. That is the baseline every project starts from

title: Your Assignment: Propose & Build
desc: The connection is proven — your job is to build something of your own on top

items: Propose your own drone-software idea — small but real; the 18 project ideas in Module 4 are your menu, or bring your own
Build a working increment on top of labs/dji-hello-world (or the official DJI sample)
Write it up: what you built, what worked, and where the SDK stopped you
Keep it achievable — a narrow feature done well beats a broad plan; the grading bar itself is defined once, in Module 4
Simulator first for anything that flies — then the SAFETY rules from the start of this module apply, every flight
Getting stuck is welcome — the error and your hypothesis become teaching material

title: The Guiding Question: Where Does the SDK End?

items: Whatever you build, find out what does NOT work — e.g. direct access to the motors or the control loop
Naming that boundary cleanly is at least as valuable for the lecture as everything that works
Compare with Module 3: a consumer SDK enforcing safety boundaries is a trust-level decision — DJI keeps your code away from the DAL-critical parts
Getting stuck is expected and welcome
Note the error message and your hypothesis about the cause
We turn exactly those notes into good exercise examples
